## 1. Goal

Create the six preset cases the website and demo rely on, each showing one behaviour, with the CSVs as master copies and a generated JavaScript data file the page reads without `fetch`. This settles O-9 (how a preset stores its capacities).

## 2. Background

**From BLUEPRINT §5 Presets:**

| Preset | What it demonstrates |
| --- | --- |
| Big-job trap | Greedy's known worst case (Fan & Liang, Lemma 4.1); its own capacities so all small jobs fit together |
| Priority starvation | Static priority starving a low-priority job; aging rescuing it |
| Memory hog | Aging alone failing for a big-memory job; reservation fixing it |
| SJF starvation | A long job starved by a stream of short ones |
| Heavy load | Many jobs, high utilization, differences in average wait |
| Tiny case | 6 to 9 jobs, compared against the exact optimum |

**From BLUEPRINT §3.4 Known worst case:**

**Known worst case (Fan & Liang, Lemma 4.1).** One huge job arrives first and fills the machine; N − 1 tiny jobs arrive a moment later, small enough to all run together. Greedy starts the huge job at once and every tiny job waits for it. The lemma is stated for weighted completion time: the competitive ratio of any priority-queue scheduler is Ω(N). For total wait the gap is even larger, because it also grows with the huge job's duration p: greedy's total wait is about (N − 1)·p, the optimum's is about the tiny jobs' duration. This case is a website preset and is stated in the report. Because our resources are integers, the preset sets its own capacities so that all N − 1 tiny jobs fit together (for example CPU capacity ≥ N − 1 with 1 core each).

## 3. Scope

**In scope:**

- Six presets: big-job trap, priority starvation, memory hog, SJF starvation, heavy load, tiny case (6–9 jobs)
- Capacities and recommended settings per preset (O-9 decides the file format)
- A command that regenerates `web/js/presets_data.js` identically
- Checking each preset shows its behaviour with the CLI

**Out of scope:**

- Website loading of presets (K-24)
- Comparison with the exact solver (K-33)

## 5. Specification

`presets_data.js` is a classic script: `window.APRM = window.APRM || {}; APRM.presetsData = [ { "name": …, "cpu_cap": …, "mem_cap": …, "jobs": [ {id, arrival, duration, cpu, mem, priority}, … ] }, … ];` — no `fetch`, works from `file://` (D31, D32).

Big-job trap (BLUEPRINT §3.4): one job using the whole machine arrives first; N − 1 tiny jobs arrive one tick later; capacities chosen so all N − 1 tiny jobs fit together (e.g. CPU capacity ≥ N − 1 with 1 core each).

## 10. Viva notes

**Idea:** each preset is a tiny story that makes one algorithmic point visible in the demo.
**Examiner question:** "Why does the big-job trap hurt greedy?" — Greedy commits to the big job at once and every small job waits for it (Fan & Liang Lemma 4.1).

## 11. Pitfalls

- A big-job trap where the small jobs cannot all fit together
- Hand-editing the generated JS file
- Using `fetch` to load CSVs
